Policy Transfer Ensures Fast Learning for Continuous-Time LQR with Entropy Regularization

Xin Guo ††thanks: UC Berkeley, IEOR. Email: xinguo@berkeley.edu    Zijiu Lyu ††thanks: UC Berkeley, IEOR. Email: zijiu.lyu@berkeley.edu
Abstract

Reinforcement Learning (RL) enables agents to learn optimal decision-making strategies through interaction with an environment, yet training from scratch on complex tasks can be highly inefficient. Transfer learning (TL), widely successful in large language models (LLMs), offers a promising direction for enhancing RL efficiency by leveraging pre-trained models.

This paper investigates policy transfer, a TL approach that initializes learning in a target RL task using a policy from a related source task, in the context of continuous-time linear quadratic regulators (LQRs) with entropy regularization. We provide the first theoretical proof of policy transfer for continuous-time RL, proving that a policy optimal for one LQR serves as a near-optimal initialization for closely related LQRs, while preserving the original algorithm’s convergence rate. Furthermore, we introduce a novel policy learning algorithm for continuous-time LQRs that achieves global linear and local super-linear convergence. Our results demonstrate both theoretical guarantees and algorithmic benefits of transfer learning in continuous-time RL, addressing a gap in existing literature and extending prior work from discrete to continuous time settings.

As a byproduct of our analysis, we derive the stability of a class of continuous-time score-based diffusion models via their connection with LQRs.

1 Introduction

Transfer learning.

Transfer learning is a machine learning technique that leverages expertise gained from one domain to enhance the learning process in another related task. It is one of the most influential techniques that underpin the capabilities of large language models (LLMs). In the context of LLMs, transfer learning involves using pre-trained models, such as those from the GPT, BERT, or similar families, that were initially trained for specific tasks. Transfer learning repurposes these models for new and related applications, often involving domain-specific variations of the original problems. See e.g. [1], [2], [3], [4], [5]. Beyond LLMs, transfer learning has also gained a significant traction in other domains, particularly for improving learning efficiency when data and computational resources are limited. See e.g. [6], [7], [8].

Reinforcement learning and transfer learning.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is one of the fundamental machine learning paradigms, where an agent learns to make a sequence of decisions by interacting with an environment and possibly with other agents. In a typical RL setup, an agent learns a policy/strategy for choosing actions in a given system state through trial and error to maximize a cumulative reward over time. However, training an agent for a complex RL task from the ground up can be extremely inefficient.

Given the exponentially growing demand for complex RL tasks, and the increasing number of pre-trained RL models for various learning tasks, it is natural to incorporate TL into RL to leverage knowledge from a pre-trained RL model to reduce both training time and computational costs, especially when there is a limited amount of data for new RL models.

Policy transfer is one of the most direct methods to leverage knowledge from one RL task to another. The basic idea of policy transfer is to use the policy learned from the source task to initialize the policy for the target task. If two RL tasks are similar, exploring the pre-trained policy as a starting point hopefully allows the agent to begin with a near-optimal strategy, with subsequent minor adjustments. This is intuitively clear and simple, and has been analyzed in a discrete-time LQ framework by [9]. Their work, as the first known theoretical studies for incorporating transfer learning into reinforcement learning, demonstrates the advantage in algorithmic performance improvement with TL technique for RL.

A natural question is, if the same benefit of transfer learning can be achieved for RL via appropriate policy transfer? Indeed, reinforcement learning, though primarily developed for discrete environment, is intrinsically continuous and complex, especially in robotics control, automatic driving, and portfolio optimization. However, analyzing transfer learning in the continuous-time RL framework remains uncharted and presents significantly greater technical challenges, as the knowledge to be transferred involves controlled stochastic processes and infinite-dimensional functional spaces.

Our work.

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of policy transfer between continuous-time linear quadratic regulators with entropy regulation (LQRs). We demonstrate that an optimal policy learned for one LQR can serve as a near-optimal policy for any closely-related LQR, while preserving at least the same convergence rate as the original learning algorithm. In addition, we propose a novel policy learning algorithm for continuous-time LQRs, which achieves a global linear convergence rate and a local super-linear convergence rate. This implies that any closely related LQR is guaranteed with a super-linear convergent learning algorithm.

Our analysis fully exploits the Gaussian structure of the optimal policy for LQRs, as well as the robustness of the associated Riccati equation. As a byproduct of our analysis, we derive the stability of a class of continuous-time score-based diffusion models via their connection with LQRs.

Related work.

The existing literature on policy learning for Linear-Quadratic (LQ) problems is extensive. For example, several studies focus on gradient-based algorithms for discrete-time LQRs. These algorithms, notably those proposed by [10] and [11], are able to achieve a global linear convergence rate in learning the parameters of the optimal feedback policy. Similarly, [12] extends this approach to continuous-time LQRs, also demonstrating a global linear convergence rate. Beyond these gradient-based methods, other research explores different aspects of LQRs. For instance, [13] develops a multistage procedure for designing a robust controller of discrete-time LQRs when the system dynamics are not fully known, while [14] introduces a model-free algorithm that directly learns the optimal policy of continuous-time LQRs, providing a theoretical guarantee with a sublinear regret bound. Furthermore, [15] provides a theoretical analysis of the sample complexity of approximate policy iteration for learning discrete-time LQRs. For a more comprehensive background, interested readers are referred to the standard references by [16] and [17].

Our work of RL with TL is inspired by [9], where a super-linear local convergent algorithm called IPO is proposed for discrete-time exploratory LQRs. In comparison, the analysis of policy transfer between continuous-time LQRs is technically more challenging. More importantly, we establish general results on policy transfer between any two closely related LQRs. The particular algorithm of IPO illustrates the benefit of policy transfer in such a context.

On the stability of continuous-time score-based diffusion models, [18] has obtained a more general result under appropriate technical assumptions. Here we derive, via connecting score-based diffusion models with LQRs, a class of models where these assumptions and hence the stability results hold.

Finally, the connection between score-based diffusion models and LQRs is well known. For example, [19] shows that a large class of generative models, including normalizing flows, score-based diffusion models, and Wasserstein gradient flows, can be viewed as the solutions to certain mean-field games (MFGs). We note that LQRs can be viewed as the degenerate case of LQMFGs. Moreover, [20] and [21] research the relationship between MFGs, Wasserstein proximals and score-based diffusion models.

2 Mathematical Formulation

Let us now set up the mathematical framework under which entropy-regularized continuous-time linear quadratic regulators (LQRs) are defined over a finite time interval [0,T][0,T].

Specifically, following the setup of [22], we assume that the state process xt∈ℝnx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} of the agent follows the linear SDE:

d​xt=[At​xt+Bt​𝔼​(ut|xt)]​d​t+σt​d​Wt,x0∼𝒟0,\displaystyle\mathrm{d}x_{t}=\Big[A_{t}x_{t}+B_{t}\mathbb{E}(u_{t}\,|\,x_{t})\Big]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad x_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}, (2.1)

where 𝔼[ut|xt]∼πt(⋅|xt)∈𝒫(ℝk)\mathbb{E}[u_{t}\,|\,x_{t}]\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x_{t})\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{k}) represents the randomized policy of the agent conditioned on xtx_{t}, (Wt)t∈[0,T](W_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} denotes the dd-dimensional standard Brownian motion (dd-BM for short), 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} denotes the initial distribution, and (At,Bt,σt)t∈[0,T](A_{t},B_{t},\sigma_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} are appropriate deterministic matrix-valued processes to be specified later.

The agent minimizes the following entropy-regularized cost function:

infπ∈𝒜Jπ(0,𝒟0):=𝔼ut∼πt(⋅|xt)[∫0Txt†Qtxt+ut†Rtut+τloght(ut|xt)dt+xT†Q′xT|x0∼𝒟0],\displaystyle\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{A}}J_{\pi}(0,\mathcal{D}_{0}):=\mathbb{E}_{u_{t}\sim\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x_{t})}\Bigg[\int_{0}^{T}x_{t}^{\dagger}Q_{t}x_{t}+u_{t}^{\dagger}R_{t}u_{t}+\tau\log h_{t}(u_{t}\,|\,x_{t})\mathrm{d}t+x_{T}^{\dagger}Q^{\prime}x_{T}\,\Bigg|\,x_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}\Bigg], (2.2)

where † denotes the transpose operator, 𝒜\mathcal{A} denotes the set of admissible randomized policies, ht(⋅|xt)h_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x_{t}) denotes the conditional probability distribution function of πt(⋅|xt)\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x_{t}), and (Qt,Rt)t∈[0,T](Q_{t},R_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} (resp. Q′Q^{\prime}) are appropriate deterministic matrix-valued processes (resp. matrix) to be specified later.

Note that the exploratory SDEs adopted here are first proposed by [22], where an entropy-regularization term is added to the cost function to encourage agent exploration.

Next, we present the technical assumptions to ensure that the above formulation (2.1) – (2.2) is well defined. In particular, our goal is to ensure that (2.1) admits a unique strong solution (see e.g. [23, Theorem 5.2.1]) and that (2.2) has a finite integrand. See [24, Section 2] for a similar setup.

Assumption 1 (Probability space).

We assume a filtered probability space (Ω,ℱ,ℙ,(ℱt)t∈[0,T])\left(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P};(\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\right) where the filtration (ℱt)t∈[0,T](\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} 1) is rich enough to support some dd-BM (Wt)t∈[0,T](W_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}, the random action (ut)t∈[0,T](u_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} of the agent, and the initial distribution 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}, which are assumed to be independent; 2) satisfies the usual conditions (i.e., ℱ0\mathcal{F}_{0} contains all the ℙ\mathbb{P}-null sets and (ℱt)t∈[0,T](\mathcal{F}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} is right-continuous).

Assumption 2 (Admissible policies).

The set 𝒜\mathcal{A} of admissible policies consists of Markovian randomized policies, i.e., the following conditions hold for any π∈𝒜\pi\in\mathcal{A}:

  1. 1.

    for any t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] and x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, πt(⋅|x)\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x) is absolutely continuous w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure on ℝk\mathbb{R}^{k} and has a finite expectation and a finite entropy;

  2. 2.

    𝔼⁡(ut|x)\mathbb{E}(u_{t}\,|\,x), when viewed as a function of (t,x)∈[0,T]×ℝn(t,x)\in[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{n}, has a linear growth w.r.t. xx and is Lipchitz continuous in xx.

Assumption 3 (Regularity conditions).

𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} is assumed to be square integrable, and

A,Q∈L∞​([0,T],ℝn×n),B∈L∞​([0,T],ℝn×k),R∈L∞([0,T],ℝk×k),σ∈L2([0,T],ℝn×d).\begin{gathered}A,Q\in L^{\infty}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}),\quad B\in L^{\infty}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}),\\ R\in L^{\infty}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}),\quad\sigma\in L^{2}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}).\end{gathered}

In addition, we assume Qt⪰0Q_{t}\succeq 0 a.e. for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], τ>0\tau>0, Q′⪰0Q^{\prime}\succeq 0, and that there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that Rt−δ​I⪰0R_{t}-\delta I\succeq 0 a.e. for t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T].

3 Transfer learning between LQRs

In this section, we consider transfer learning between continuous-time linear quadratic regulators with entropy regulation (LQRs).

More specifically, suppose that there are two LQRs whose system parameters are (θt)t∈[0,T](\theta_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} and (θ~t)t∈[0,T](\tilde{\theta}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}, respectively. Without loss of generality, let us assume that the first LQR is more accessible and easier to learn, and let us denote by (Kt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} the parameter of its optimal policy. We will show that if (θt)t∈[0,T](\theta_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} and (θ~t)t∈[0,T](\tilde{\theta}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} are sufficiently close, then (Kt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} may be used as an initialization to efficiently learn the optimal policy of the second LQR. Here in our framework the parameters θ=(A,Q,B,R,Q′)\theta=(A,Q,B,R,Q^{\prime}).

Theorem 1 (Transfer learning of LQRs).

Given an LQR represented by model parameters θ\theta, for which there exists an optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} and an associated learning algorithm. Now, suppose there is a new LQR represented by model parameters θ~\tilde{\theta}. Then, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0, such that with an appropriate initialization π(0)\pi^{(0)}, this learning algorithm has the same convergence rate and finds a near-optimal policy of the new LQR, provided that

d⁡(π(0),π∗)+d⁡(θ~,θ)<ϵ.d(\pi^{(0)},\pi^{\ast})+d(\tilde{\theta},\theta)<\epsilon.

Here dd denotes an appropriately chosen distance on the corresponding metric space.

This result is based on the following two lemmas. First, we see that the optimal randomized policy of the LQR defined by (2.1) – (2.2) can be derived via the dynamic programming principle (DPP) and by following a similar calculation from the earlier work [22] and [24].

Lemma 2.

The optimal randomized policy of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2) is:

πt∗(⋅|x)\displaystyle\pi^{\ast}_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x) =𝒩⁡(−Rt−1​Bt†​Pt​x,τ2​Rt−1),\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}\left(-R_{t}^{-1}B_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}x,\,\frac{\tau}{2}R_{t}^{-1}\right), (3.1)

where PtP_{t} solves the following Riccati equation:

d​Ptd​t+At†​Pt+Pt​At+Qt−Pt​Bt​Rt−1​Bt†​Pt\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}P_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+A_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}+P_{t}A_{t}+Q_{t}-P_{t}B_{t}R^{-1}_{t}B_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t} =0,PT=Q′.\displaystyle=0,\quad P_{T}=Q^{\prime}. (3.2)
Remark 1.

The Gaussian form of π∗\pi^{\ast} originates from the entropy-regularization term in the cost function (2.2). The mean of π∗\pi^{\ast} appears in a mean-reverting fashion, pushing the agent to 0. Meanwhile, the covariance of π∗\pi^{\ast} is driven by the regularization coefficient τ>0\tau>0. The larger the value of τ\tau, the more the agent would explore. In the case where τ→0+\tau\rightarrow 0^{+}, π∗\pi^{\ast} would converge to a deterministic policy as one should expect (see [22, Section 5.4] for a formal discussion on the convergence of π∗\pi^{\ast}).

Lemma 3 (Key lemma).

Under Assumption 3, denote by ℛ\mathcal{R} the solution map of the Riccati equation (3.2), i.e.,

ℛ:L∞​([0,T],ℝn×n)×L∞​([0,T],S≥0n)\displaystyle\mathcal{R}:L^{\infty}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n\times n})\times L^{\infty}([0,T],S^{n}_{\geq 0}) ×L∞​([0,T],ℝn×k)×L∞​([0,T],S>0k)×S≥0n\displaystyle\times L^{\infty}([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n\times k})\times L^{\infty}([0,T],S^{k}_{>0})\times S^{n}_{\geq 0}
⟶C⁡([0,T],S≥0n)\displaystyle\longrightarrow C([0,T],S^{n}_{\geq 0})
(At∈[0,T],Qt∈[0,T],Bt∈[0,T],Rt∈[0,T],Q′)\displaystyle(A_{t\in[0,T]},Q_{t\in[0,T]},B_{t\in[0,T]},R_{t\in[0,T]},Q^{\prime}) ⟼ℛ⁡(A,Q,B,R,Q′):=(Pt)t∈[0,T].\displaystyle\longmapsto\mathcal{R}(A,Q,B,R,Q^{\prime}):=(P_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}.

Then, ℛ\mathcal{R} is continuous, where the L∞L^{\infty} (resp. S≥0nS^{n}_{\geq 0}) space is equipped with the functional ||⋅||∞;[0,T]||\cdot||_{\infty;[0,T]} norm (resp. matrix 2-norm).

Now, Theorem 1 follows immediately from Lemma 3. Indeed, by Lemma 3, the optimal policy is a continuous function in the LQR’s model parameters. As a result, when the distance between θ~\tilde{\theta} and θ\theta is small enough, the optimal policies of the two LQRs can be made arbitrarily close to each other. This implies the desired near-optimality.

4 IPO and its super-linear convergence for LQRs

Now we design an Iterative Policy Optimization (IPO) learning algorithm for LQRs. We will first establish its global linear convergence, and then show its super-linear convergence when the initial policy lies in a certain neighborhood of the optimal policy. As a corollary, in the context of transfer learning, we will see that such an algorithm yields an optimal policy for any closely related LQR with an appropriate initialization (i.e., policy transfer). Our algorithm is analogous to the IPO algorithm developed for discrete-time LQRs in [9], hence the adopted name IPO.

The algorithm and the analysis rely crucially on the Gaussian form of the LQR’s optimal policy. Indeed, given the special form of (3.1), it suffices to optimize only within the following class of Gaussian policies:

πt(⋅|x)=𝒩(−Ktx,Σt),\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x)=\mathcal{N}(-K_{t}x,\,\Sigma_{t}), (4.1)

which admits the following analytical solution:

KtIPO\displaystyle K^{\rm IPO}_{t} =Rt−1​Bt†​PtK,\displaystyle=R_{t}^{-1}B_{t}^{\dagger}P^{K}_{t}, (IPO: KK)
ΣtIPO\displaystyle\Sigma_{t}^{\rm IPO} =τ2​Rt−1.\displaystyle=\frac{\tau}{2}R^{-1}_{t}. (IPO: Σ\Sigma)

where PtKP^{K}_{t} is the solution to (4.4). Notice that ΣtIPO\Sigma^{\rm IPO}_{t} reaches the covariance of the optimal Gaussian policy after a single iteration (cf. (4.2)). We present below the IPO algorithm for updating KtK_{t}.

Convergence of IPO.

Now we present the convergence results of the IPO algorithm defined by (IPO: K ) – (IPO: Σ ). We will show that with an additional assumption stated in Assumption 4 , the IPO algorithm has a global linear convergence rate. Since (ΣtIPO)t∈[0,T](\Sigma^{\rm IPO}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} always reaches the covariance of the optimal Gaussian policy after a single iteration, we only discuss the convergence of (KtIPO)t∈[0,T](K^{\rm IPO}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}.

For any given parameters (Kt,Σt)t∈[0,T](K_{t},\Sigma_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}, we use the cost function value to measure their goodness (with an abuse of notation):

C⁡(K,Σ)\displaystyle C(K,\Sigma) :=JπK,Σ​(0,𝒟0)\displaystyle:=J_{\pi_{K,\Sigma}}(0,\mathcal{D}_{0}) (4.8)
=𝔼⁡(x†​P0K​x+r0K,Σ|x∼𝒟0),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left(x^{\dagger}P^{K}_{0}x+r^{K,\Sigma}_{0}\,\Big|\,x\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}\right),

where (PtK,rtK,Σ)t∈[0,T](P^{K}_{t},r^{K,\Sigma}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} solves the coupled Riccati equations (4.4) – (4.5). Note that C⁡(K,Σ)C(K,\Sigma) is minimized at (Kt∗,Σt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t},\Sigma^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} (resp. at (Kt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} when viewed only as a functional in KK). See (4.2) for the values of (Kt∗,Σt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t},\Sigma^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}.

Assumption 4.

𝔼⁡(x0​x0†|x0∼𝒟0)≻0\mathbb{E}\big(x_{0}x_{0}^{\dagger}\,\big|\,x_{0}\sim\mathcal{D}_{0}\big)\succ 0.

Theorem 4 (Global linear convergence of IPO).

Under Assumptions 1 – 4, suppose that {(Kt(i),Σt)t∈[0,T]}i≥0\{(K^{(i)}_{t},\Sigma_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\}_{i\geq 0} is a sequence of parameters following the algorithm (IPO: K ). Then, there exist constants 𝒞1K>0\mathcal{C}^{K}_{1}>0 and 0≤𝒞1<10\leq\mathcal{C}_{1}<1, which depend on K(0)K^{(0)} and the data of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2), such that:

∀i≥0,𝒞1K​∫0T||Kt(i+1)−Kt∗||22​𝑑t≤C⁡(K(i+1),Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)≤𝒞1​[C⁡(K(i),Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)].\displaystyle\forall i\geq 0,\quad\mathcal{C}^{K}_{1}\int_{0}^{T}\left|\left|K^{(i+1)}_{t}-K^{\ast}_{t}\right|\right|_{2}^{2}\mathrm{d}t\leq C(K^{(i+1)},\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\leq\mathcal{C}_{1}\left[C(K^{(i)},\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\right].

One can further establish a super-linear convergence rate for the IPO algorithm, with an appropriate initialization.

Theorem 5 (Local super-linear convergence of IPO).

Under Assumptions 1 – 4, there exist constants (ϵ,𝒞2)>0(\epsilon,\mathcal{C}_{2})>0, which depend on the data of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2), such that for any sequence of parameters {(Kt(i),Σt)t∈[0,T]}i≥0\{(K^{(i)}_{t},\Sigma_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}\}_{i\geq 0} following the algorithm (IPO: K ) and satisfying:

∫0T||Kt(0)−Kt∗||22​𝑑t≤ϵ,\int_{0}^{T}\left|\left|K^{(0)}_{t}-K^{\ast}_{t}\right|\right|_{2}^{2}\mathrm{d}t\leq\epsilon,

the following local super-linear convergence holds:

∀i≥0,C⁡(K(i+1),Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)≤𝒞2​[C⁡(K(i),Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)]32.\forall i\geq 0,\quad C(K^{(i+1)},\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\leq\mathcal{C}_{2}\left[C(K^{(i)},\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\right]^{\frac{3}{2}}.
Remark 2.

Assumption 4 is critical in proving that the minimum eigenvalue of 𝔼⁡(xt​xt†)\mathbb{E}(x_{t}x_{t}^{\dagger}) is uniformly bounded away from 0 (cf. Lemma 11). This uniform lower bound then leads to the uniform contraction of the IPO algorithm. In the discrete-time setting (cf. [9]), the counterpart of Assumption 4 is also imposed to guarantee the global linear convergence of the algorithms (cf. [9, Lemma 5.2]).

Remark 3.

In fact, one can replace 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} with any square-integrable distribution in the definition of C⁡(⋅,⋅)C(\cdot,\cdot) (cf. (4.8)) and all the above convergence results still hold. This is because the initial distribution of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2) is irrelevant to the definition of the IPO algorithm. In this case, one only needs to change the statement of Assumption 4 to guarantee the corresponding positive-definiteness.

Transfer learning with IPO.

Now combining Theorem 1 and Theorem 5, we have immediately the super-fast learning via appropriate policy transfer between LQRs. We mention that in Theorem 5, ϵ\epsilon admits a lower bound which only depends on the norms of the LQR’s model parameters.

Corollary 6 (Transfer learning of LQRs with IPO).

Under Assumptions 1 – 4, denote by (Kt∗)t∈[0,T](K^{\ast}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} the parameter of the optimal Gaussian policy of the LQR represented by (At∈[0,T],Qt∈[0,T],Bt∈[0,T],Rt∈[0,T],Q′)(A_{t\in[0,T]},Q_{t\in[0,T]},B_{t\in[0,T]},R_{t\in[0,T]},Q^{\prime}). Then, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0, such that any initialization (Kt(0))t∈[0,T](K^{(0)}_{t})_{t\in[0,T]} converges with a super-linear convergence rate to the optimal Gaussian policy of any LQR represented by (A~t∈[0,T],Q~t∈[0,T],B~t∈[0,T],R~t∈[0,T],Q′~)(\tilde{A}_{t\in[0,T]},\tilde{Q}_{t\in[0,T]},\tilde{B}_{t\in[0,T]},\tilde{R}_{t\in[0,T]},\tilde{Q^{\prime}}), provided that

‖K(0)−K∗‖2;[0,T]+‖A~−A‖∞;[0,T]+||Q~−Q||∞;[0,T]+‖B~−B‖∞;[0,T]+||R~−R||∞;[0,T]+‖Q′~−Q′‖2<ϵ,||K^{(0)}-K^{\ast}||_{2;[0,T]}+||\tilde{A}-A||_{\infty;[0,T]}+||\tilde{Q}-Q||_{\infty;[0,T]}\\ +||\tilde{B}-B||_{\infty;[0,T]}+||\tilde{R}-R||_{\infty;[0,T]}+||\tilde{Q^{\prime}}-Q^{\prime}||_{2}<\epsilon,

where ||⋅||∞;[0,T]||\cdot||_{\infty;[0,T]} (resp. ||⋅||2;[0,T]||\cdot||_{2;[0,T]}, ||⋅||2||\cdot||_{2}) denotes the functional L∞L^{\infty} norm (resp. functional L2L^{2} norm, matrix 2-norm).

5 Application: stability of score-based diffusion models

In this section, we will show that our analysis of LQRs, especially the key Lemma 3 can be applied to obtain the stability of score-based diffusion models. The critical observation is that the probability density function of (a certain class of) score-based diffusion models can be found in the LQRs under the optimal randomized policy. This allows us to consider a class of score matching functions and to bound the distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution.

In the rest of this section, we always impose the following assumption on the LQR (2.1) – (2.2).

Assumption 5.

We assume

tr⁡(At)=−τ4​log⁡|Rt|(τ​π)k,Bt​Rt−1​Bt†=σt​σt†,Qt=0\displaystyle\tr(A_{t})=-\frac{\tau}{4}\log\frac{|R_{t}|}{(\tau\pi)^{k}},\quad B_{t}R_{t}^{-1}B_{t}^{\dagger}=\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t}^{\dagger},\quad Q_{t}=0

for any t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T], and Q′≻0Q^{\prime}\succ 0.

Mechanism of score-based diffusion models.

Score-based diffusion models have become the SOTA solution to various tasks in different areas. For completeness, we first recall their basic mechanism briefly. (See e.g. [18] for a comprehensive review).

Suppose p0datap^{\rm data}_{0} is the distribution that one aims to generate. Diffusion model starts by defining a forward SDE (e.g. an OU process) over [0,T][0,T] with the initial distribution p0datap^{\rm data}_{0}. Denote by ss and pTdatap^{\rm data}_{T} the score function and the terminal distribution of the forward SDE, respectively. Then, in the sampling stage, a backward SDE, whose dynamics depend on ss and whose initial distribution is pTdatap^{\rm data}_{T}, is simulated. (Figure 1 summarizes the basic mechanism of score-based diffusion models).

Theoretically, it can be shown that the terminal distribution of the backward SDE is equal to p0datap^{\rm data}_{0}. In practice, however, ss and pTdatap^{\rm data}_{T} are typically not accessible, and a score matching function sβs_{\beta} and a noise distribution pnoisep^{\rm noise} are adopted as their approximations, respectively. Denote by p≈datap^{\rm data}_{\approx} the terminal distribution of the backward SDE (under sβs_{\beta} and pnoisep^{\rm noise}).

Connection with LQRs.

Next, we recall the connection between score-based diffusion models and LQRs. Our Lemma 7 can be viewed as a special case of [19, Theorem 7]. The key ingredient is the Cole-Hopf transformation for the HJB equation that characterizes the optimal policy of the LQR (cf. (6.2) in our case).

Lemma 7.

Under Assumptions 1 – 3 and 5, the probability density function, which is denoted by p^​(t,x)\hat{p}(t,x), of the following diffusion process on [0,T][0,T]:

d​X^t=−AT−t​X^t​d​t+σT−t​d​Wt,X^0∼𝒩⁡(0,(Q′)−1)\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\hat{X}_{t}=-A_{T-t}\hat{X}_{t}\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{T-t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad\hat{X}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,(Q^{\prime})^{-1}\right) (5.1)

can be expressed by:

p^​(t,x)=(2​π)−n2​|Q′|12​exp⁡[−12​J​(T−t,x)],\displaystyle\hat{p}(t,x)=(2\pi)^{-\frac{n}{2}}|Q^{\prime}|^{\frac{1}{2}}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}J(T-t,x)\right],

where J⁡(t,x)=x†​Pt​x+rtJ(t,x)=x^{\dagger}P_{t}x+r_{t} with (Pt,rt)(P_{t},r_{t}) solving the coupled Riccati equations (3.2) – (6.3).

We note that (5.1) specifies a diffusion model where the data distribution X^0\hat{X}_{0} (i.e., the distribution one aims to generate) is Gaussian, and the forward SDE is an OU process. By Lemma 7, p^​(t,x)\hat{p}(t,x) is determined by PT−tP_{T-t} and rT−tr_{T-t}. In fact, p^​(t,x)\hat{p}(t,x) is determined solely by PT−tP_{T-t} since the spacial integral of p^​(t,x)\hat{p}(t,x) must be 1. As a result, the score function of (5.1) (i.e., the gradient of log⁡p^​(t,x)\log\hat{p}(t,x)) is determined by PT−tP_{T-t}.

A class of score matching functions and the stability.

Now, the backward SDE of (5.1) is:

dY^t=[AtY^t+σtσt†∇logp^Q′(T−t,Y^t)]dt+σtdWt,Y^0∼p^Q′(T,⋅),\displaystyle\mathrm{d}\hat{Y}_{t}=\left[A_{t}\hat{Y}_{t}+\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t}^{\dagger}\nabla\log\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}(T-t,\hat{Y}_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad\hat{Y}_{0}\sim\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}(T,\cdot), (5.2)

where we use p^Q′\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}} to indicate the dependence of p^\hat{p} on Q′Q^{\prime}.

In practice, when p^Q′\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}} is not explicitly known, a score matching function ss is used as an approximator of ∇log⁡p^Q′\nabla\log\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}, and the initial distribution is approximated by some noise distribution pnoisep^{\rm noise}, i.e.,

d​Yt=[At​Yt+σt​σt†​s​(T−t,Yt)]​d​t+σt​d​Wt,Y0∼pnoise.\displaystyle\mathrm{d}Y_{t}=\left[A_{t}Y_{t}+\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t}^{\dagger}s(T-t,Y_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t+\sigma_{t}\mathrm{d}W_{t},\quad Y_{0}\sim p^{\text{noise}}. (5.3)

We will show that YT≈Y^T​=𝑑​X^0Y_{T}\approx\hat{Y}_{T}\overset{d}{=}\hat{X}_{0} when s≈∇log⁡p^Q′s\approx\nabla\log\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}} and pnoise≈p^Q′​(T,⋅)p^{\text{noise}}\approx\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}(T,\cdot): this follows from the stability of the Riccati equation (3.2) (cf. Lemma 3), such that s=∇log⁡p^Ms=\nabla\log\hat{p}^{M} serves as a good score matching function as long as M≈Q′M\approx Q^{\prime}.

Theorem 8 (Error bound analysis).

Under Assumptions 1 – 3 and 5, there exist constants (C1,C2,C3)>0(C_{1},C_{2},C_{3})>0, which depend on the data of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2), such that for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists δ0>0\delta_{0}>0, such that ‖M−Q′‖<δ0||M-Q^{\prime}||<\delta_{0} implies

dTV​(YT,Y^T)≤dTV​(pnoise,p^Q′​(T,⋅))+C1​ϵ,d_{\rm TV}\left(Y_{T},\hat{Y}_{T}\right)\leq d_{\rm TV}\left(p^{\rm noise},\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}(T,\cdot)\right)+C_{1}\epsilon,

and

W2​(YT,Y^T)≤C2​W22​(pnoise,p^Q′​(T,⋅))+C3​ϵ2,W_{2}\left(Y_{T},\hat{Y}_{T}\right)\leq\sqrt{C_{2}W_{2}^{2}\left(p^{\rm noise},\hat{p}^{Q^{\prime}}(T,\cdot)\right)+C_{3}\epsilon^{2}},

where YtY_{t} satisfies (5.3) with s=∇log⁡p^Ms=\nabla\log\hat{p}^{M}, and Y^t\hat{Y}_{t} satisfies (5.2). Here dTVd_{\rm TV} and W2W_{2} to denote the total variation distance and 2-Wasserstein distance, respectively.

Proof.

Our proof utilizes the results in [18, Section 5]. We first prove the total variation bound. By Lemma 3, for any fixed x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, we have:

∇log⁡qM​(⋅,x)→∇log⁡qQ′​(⋅,x)​ in ​C​([0,T],ℝn)\nabla\log q^{M}(\cdot,x)\rightarrow\nabla\log q^{Q^{\prime}}(\cdot,x)\text{ in }C([0,T],\mathbb{R}^{n})

as M→Q′M\rightarrow Q^{\prime}. Then, by probability theory, we have:

∀t∈[0,T],𝔼X^t∼q⁡(t,⋅)​‖∇log⁡qM​(t,X^t)−∇log⁡qQ′​(t,X^t)‖2→0\forall t\in[0,T],\quad\mathbb{E}_{\hat{X}_{t}\sim q(t,\cdot)}\Big|\Big|\nabla\log q^{M}(t,\hat{X}_{t})-\nabla\log q^{Q^{\prime}}(t,\hat{X}_{t})\Big|\Big|^{2}\rightarrow 0

as M→Q′M\rightarrow Q^{\prime}. The total variation bound is then proved by invoking [18, Theorem 5.2]. Similarly, the 2-Wasserstein bound can be proved by invoking [18, Theorem 5.5 and Eqn. (5.13)]. ∎

Conclusion.

Linear-Quadratic (LQ) control problems are a cornerstone of classical control theory. Our analysis of transfer learning for LQRs benefits from its analytical tractability and gains critical insights for general continuous-time RL problems. In particular, it shows that transfer learning will be valuable for leveraging existing RL algorithms beyond LQR framework. The precise mathematical analysis relies on studies of stability and continuity of optimal policy for stochastic control problems. The analysis on LQRs also leads to the stability results for a class of score-based continuous-time diffusion models.

6 Appendix

6.1 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof.

Define the following intermediate cost function:

J(t,x):=infπ∈𝒜𝔼us∼πs(⋅|xs)[∫tTxs†Qsxs+us†Rsus+τloghs(us|xs)ds+xT†Q′xT|xt=x].\displaystyle J(t,x):=\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{u_{s}\sim\pi_{s}(\cdot\,|\,x_{s})}\Bigg[\int_{t}^{T}x_{s}^{\dagger}Q_{s}x_{s}+u_{s}^{\dagger}R_{s}u_{s}+\tau\log h_{s}(u_{s}\,|\,x_{s})\mathrm{d}s+x_{T}^{\dagger}Q^{\prime}x_{T}\,\Bigg|\,x_{t}=x\Bigg]. (6.1)

Then, DPP produces the following HJB equation of the LQR (2.1) – (2.2):

−∂J⁡(t,x)∂t=infπ∈𝒜𝔼ut∼πt{(Atx+Btu¯t)⋅∇J(t,x)+12(σtσt†)⋅ΔJ(t,x)+x†Qtx+ut†Rtut+τloght(ut|x)},J(T,x)=x†Q′x,-\frac{\partial J(t,x)}{\partial t}=\inf_{\pi\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}_{u_{t}\sim\pi_{t}}\Bigg\{(A_{t}x+B_{t}\bar{u}_{t})\cdot\nabla J(t,x)+\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t}^{\dagger})\cdot\Delta J(t,x)\\ +x^{\dagger}Q_{t}x+u_{t}^{\dagger}R_{t}u_{t}+\tau\log h_{t}(u_{t}\,|\,x)\Bigg\},\quad J(T,x)=x^{\dagger}Q^{\prime}x, (6.2)

where we use ⋅¯\bar{\cdot} to imply the expectation of the underlying random variable/distribution, and ht(⋅|x)h_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x) denotes the (conditional) probability distribution function of the Markov randomized policy πt(⋅|x)\pi_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x).

By [9, Lemma 2.2], the RHS of (6.2) is minimized by the following Gaussian policy:

πt∗(⋅|x)=𝒩(−12Rt−1Bt†∇J(t,x),τ2Rt−1).\pi^{\ast}_{t}(\cdot\,|\,x)=\mathcal{N}\left(-\frac{1}{2}R_{t}^{-1}B_{t}^{\dagger}\nabla J(t,x),\,\frac{\tau}{2}R_{t}^{-1}\right).

Observing the linear quadratic nature of LQRs, we introduce the following ansatz for J⁡(t,x)J(t,x):

J⁡(t,x)\displaystyle J(t,x) =x†​Pt​x+rt.\displaystyle=x^{\dagger}P_{t}x+r_{t}.

After plugging the ansatz for JJ and the expression of π∗\pi^{\ast} into (6.2), we obtain the following coupled Riccati equations for (Pt,rt)(P_{t},r_{t}):

d​Ptd​t+At†​Pt+Pt​At+Qt−Pt​Bt​Rt−1​Bt†​Pt\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}P_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+A_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}+P_{t}A_{t}+Q_{t}-P_{t}B_{t}R^{-1}_{t}B_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t} =0,PT=Q′,\displaystyle=0,\quad P_{T}=Q^{\prime}, (3.2)
d​rtd​t+tr⁡(σt†​Pt​σt)+τ2​log⁡|Rt|(τ​π)k\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}r_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+\tr(\sigma_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}\sigma_{t})+\frac{\tau}{2}\log\frac{|R_{t}|}{(\tau\pi)^{k}} =0,rT=0.\displaystyle=0,\quad r_{T}=0. (6.3)

Hence the lemma. ∎

6.2 Appendix B: Proof of Lemma 3

Proof.

The well-definedness of ℛ\mathcal{R} is guaranteed by [25, Corollary 2.10]. For simplicity, in the rest we only prove the continuity of ℛ\mathcal{R} with respect to (At,Bt)t∈[0,T](A_{t},B_{t})_{t\in[0,T]}. The continuity with respect to the rest arguments can be proved by the same route.

For any (At,Bt)(A_{t},B_{t}) (resp. (A~t,B~)(\tilde{A}_{t},\tilde{B})), we denote by PtP_{t} (resp. P~t\tilde{P}_{t}) the solution of (3.2). Define Δ​Pt:=Pt−P~t\Delta P_{t}:=P_{t}-\tilde{P}_{t}. It can be shown that Δ​Pt\Delta P_{t} satisfies the ODE:

d​Δ​Ptd​t+At†​Δ​Pt+(At−A~t)†​P~t+Δ​Pt​At+P~t​(At−A~t)−(Pt​Bt​Rt−1​Bt†​Pt−P~t​B~t​Rt−1​B~t†​P~t)\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\Delta P_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}+A_{t}^{\dagger}\Delta P_{t}+(A_{t}-\tilde{A}_{t})^{\dagger}\tilde{P}_{t}+\Delta P_{t}A_{t}+\tilde{P}_{t}(A_{t}-\tilde{A}_{t})-(P_{t}B_{t}R^{-1}_{t}B_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}-\tilde{P}_{t}\tilde{B}_{t}R^{-1}_{t}{\tilde{B}_{t}}^{\dagger}\tilde{P}_{t}) =0,\displaystyle=0,
Δ​PT\displaystyle\Delta P_{T} =0.\displaystyle=0.

By integrating over [t,T][t,T] and then taking the matrix 2-norm on both sides, we obtain:

‖Δ​Pt‖2≤∫tT[2​||As||2+δ|​|Bs||22​(‖Ps‖2+||P~s||2)]​||Δ​Ps||2​𝑑s+2|​|A−A~||∫tT∞;[0,T]||P~s||2​𝑑s+2​δ||B−B~||∞;[0,T]​∫tT(‖Bs‖2​‖Ps‖2+‖B~s‖2||P~s||2)||P~s||2​ds,||\Delta P_{t}||_{2}\leq\int_{t}^{T}\Big[2||A_{s}||_{2}+\delta||B_{s}||_{2}^{2}(||P_{s}||_{2}+||\tilde{P}_{s}||_{2})\Big]||\Delta P_{s}||_{2}\mathrm{d}s+2||A-\tilde{A}||_{\infty;[0,T]}\int_{t}^{T}||\tilde{P}_{s}||_{2}\mathrm{d}s\\ +2\delta||B-\tilde{B}||_{\infty;[0,T]}\int_{t}^{T}(||B_{s}||_{2}||P_{s}||_{2}+||\tilde{B}_{s}||_{2}||\tilde{P}_{s}||_{2})||\tilde{P}_{s}||_{2}\mathrm{d}s, (6.4)

where δ>0\delta>0 is defined in Assumption 3. Notice that ‖P‖∞;[0,T]||P||_{\infty;[0,T]} (resp. ‖P~‖∞;[0,T]||\tilde{P}||_{\infty;[0,T]}) can be controlled by ‖A‖∞;[0,T]+‖B‖∞;[0,T]||A||_{\infty;[0,T]}+||B||_{\infty;[0,T]} (resp. ‖A~‖∞;[0,T]+‖B~‖∞;[0,T]||\tilde{A}||_{\infty;[0,T]}+||\tilde{B}||_{\infty;[0,T]}), applying Gronwall’s inequality on (6.4) finishes the proof. ∎

6.3 Proof of Theorem 4

In the following, with an abuse of notation, we sometimes use ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle to indicate the usual matrix inner product. In addition, for any matrix MM, we use λmin​(M)\lambda_{\min}(M) (resp. ‖M‖2||M||_{2}) to denote the square root of the smallest (resp. largest) eigenvalue of M†​MM^{\dagger}M.

We first define the following matrix-valued functions.

𝒢⁡(t,K′,K)\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(t,K^{\prime},K) :=PtK​[Bt​(Kt−Kt′)]+[Bt​(Kt−Kt′)]†​PtK+K′t†​Rt​Kt′−Kt†​Rt​Kt,\displaystyle:=P^{K}_{t}\big[B_{t}(K_{t}-K^{\prime}_{t})\big]+\big[B_{t}(K_{t}-K^{\prime}_{t})\big]^{\dagger}P^{K}_{t}+{K^{\prime}}^{\dagger}_{t}R_{t}K^{\prime}_{t}-K^{\dagger}_{t}R_{t}K_{t},

Since Kt∗=Rt−1​Bt†​Pt∗K_{t}^{\ast}=R^{-1}_{t}B_{t}^{\dagger}P_{t}^{\ast}, we have 𝒢⁡(t,K,K∗)=(Kt−Kt∗)†​Rt​(Kt−Kt∗)⪰0.\mathcal{G}(t,K,K^{\ast})=(K_{t}-K^{\ast}_{t})^{\dagger}R_{t}(K_{t}-K^{\ast}_{t})\succeq 0. Also, it can be verified by algebraic calculation that G⁡(t,K)⪰0G(t,K)\succeq 0. In addition, for notational simplicity, in the rest of this section, we define

yt:=𝔼⁡(xt​xt†),\displaystyle y_{t}:=\mathbb{E}(x_{t}x_{t}^{\dagger}), (✡)

where xtx_{t} solves the state SDE (2.1) with utu_{t} following the policy πt=𝒩⁡(−Kt​x,Σt)\pi_{t}=\mathcal{N}(-K_{t}x,\Sigma_{t}). And we shall use superscripts to indicate different policies. For instance, by yt′y^{\prime}_{t} we imply that yt′=𝔼⁡(xt′​(xt′)†)y^{\prime}_{t}=\mathbb{E}\left(x^{\prime}_{t}(x^{\prime}_{t})^{\dagger}\right) where xt′x^{\prime}_{t} solves the state SDE (2.1) with utu_{t} following the policy πt=𝒩⁡(−Kt′​x,Σt)\pi_{t}=\mathcal{N}(-K^{\prime}_{t}x,\Sigma_{t}).

The proof of the global linear convergence relies on the following lemmas.

Lemma 9 (Cost difference).

Under Assumptions 1 – 3, the cost difference of two parametrized Gaussian policies is given by:

C⁡(K′,Σ)−C⁡(K,Σ)=∫0T⟨yt′,𝒢⁡(t,K′,K)⟩​𝑑t,C(K^{\prime},\Sigma)-C(K,\Sigma)=\int_{0}^{T}\Big\langle y^{\prime}_{t},\mathcal{G}(t,K^{\prime},K)\Big\rangle\mathrm{d}t,

where yt′y^{\prime}_{t} is defined by (✡ ‣ 6.3).

Proof.

For notational simplicity, denote J′​(t,x):=JK′,Σ​(t,x)J^{\prime}(t,x):=J_{K^{\prime},\Sigma}(t,x) and J⁡(t,x):=JK,Σ​(t,x)J(t,x):=J^{K,\Sigma}(t,x). By subtracting the two Bellman equations that J′​(t,x)J^{\prime}(t,x) and J⁡(t,x)J(t,x) satisfy (cf. (4.3)), we obtain:

∂(J′−J)∂t+[(At−Bt​Kt′)​x]⋅∇(J′−J)+12​(σt​σt†)⋅Δ⁡(J′−J)+F⁡(t,x)=0,\displaystyle\frac{\partial(J^{\prime}-J)}{\partial t}+\big[(A_{t}-B_{t}K_{t}^{\prime})x\big]\cdot\nabla(J^{\prime}-J)+\frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{t}\sigma_{t}^{\dagger})\cdot\Delta(J^{\prime}-J)+F(t,x)=0,

where

F⁡(t,x)=[Bt​(Kt−Kt′)​x]⋅∇J+(K′​x)†​R​(K′​x)−(K​x)†​R​(K​x).F(t,x)=\big[B_{t}(K_{t}-K_{t}^{\prime})x\big]\cdot\nabla J+(K^{\prime}x)^{\dagger}R(K^{\prime}x)-(Kx)^{\dagger}R(Kx).

Define u⁡(t,x):=J′​(t,x)−J⁡(t,x)u(t,x):=J^{\prime}(t,x)-J(t,x). By Ito’s formula:

𝔼⁡[d​u​(t,xt′)]=𝔼⁡[F⁡(t,xt′)]​d​t,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{d}u(t,x_{t}^{\prime})\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[F(t,x^{\prime}_{t})\big]\mathrm{d}t,

where xt′x_{t}^{\prime} solves the state SDE (2.1) with utu_{t} following the policy πt′=𝒩⁡(−Kt′​x,Σt)\pi^{\prime}_{t}=\mathcal{N}(-K^{\prime}_{t}x,\Sigma_{t}). Finally, by integrating on [0,T][0,T], we have:

C⁡(K′,Σ)−C⁡(K,Σ)\displaystyle C(K^{\prime},\Sigma)-C(K,\Sigma) =−𝔼⁡[∫0Td​u​(t,xt′)]\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\mathrm{d}u(t,x_{t}^{\prime})\right]
=𝔼⁡[∫0TF⁡(t,xt′)​𝑑t].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}F(t,x^{\prime}_{t})\mathrm{d}t\right].

A manipulation of the matrices finishes the proof. ∎

Under Assumptions 1 – 4, suppose K′K^{\prime} is the one-step update of KK following the algorithm (IPO: K ). Then,

C⁡(K′,Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)≤{1−mint∈[0,T]⁡λmin​(yt′)maxt∈[0,T]⁡‖yt∗‖2}​[C⁡(K,Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)],C(K^{\prime},\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\leq\left\{1-\frac{\min_{t\in[0,T]}\lambda_{\min}(y^{\prime}_{t})}{\max_{t\in[0,T]}||y^{\ast}_{t}||_{2}}\right\}\big[C(K,\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\big],

≤∫0T‖yt∗‖2​tr⁡[G⁡(t,K)]​𝑑t,\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{T}||y^{\ast}_{t}||_{2}\tr\big[G(t,K)\big]\mathrm{d}t,
≤maxt∈[0,T]||yt∗||∫0T2⁡tr⁡[G⁡(t,K)]​𝑑t.\displaystyle\leq\max_{t\in[0,T]}||y^{\ast}_{t}||_{2}\int_{0}^{T}\tr\big[G(t,K)\big]\mathrm{d}t.

≤−mint∈[0,T]λmin(yt′)∫0Ttr[G(t,K)]dt\displaystyle\leq-\min_{t\in[0,T]}\lambda_{\min}(y^{\prime}_{t})\int_{0}^{T}\tr\big[G(t,K)\big]\mathrm{d}t
≤−mint∈[0,T]⁡λmin​(yt′)maxt∈[0,T]⁡‖yt∗‖2​[C⁡(K,Σ)−C⁡(K∗,Σ)].\displaystyle\leq-\frac{\min_{t\in[0,T]}\lambda_{\min}(y^{\prime}_{t})}{\max_{t\in[0,T]}||y^{\ast}_{t}||_{2}}\big[C(K,\Sigma)-C(K^{\ast},\Sigma)\big].

Lemma 11 (Lower bound of λmin\lambda_{\min}).

Under Assumptions 1 – 4, suppose {(K(i),Σ)}i≥0\left\{\left(K^{(i)},\Sigma\right)\right\}_{i\geq 0} is a sequence of parameters following the algorithm (IPO: K ). Then, there exists μ¯>0\underline{\mu}>0, which is affected by K(0)K^{(0)}, such that:
